items.prompt: All sounds are made by something that is ___.

options.why: Melting is a change of state, not how sound is made.
Glowing gives light, not sound.
Freezing is a change of state, not how sound is made.

hints: Touch your throat while you hum.
What do you feel?
Something is moving very quickly back and forth.
items.explanation: Every sound is made by something vibrating, which means moving quickly back and forth.

items.prompt: Grains of rice on a drum jump when the drum is hit. What does this show?

options.text: The rice is making the sound.
options.why: The rice only shows that the drum skin is moving.
Magnets have nothing to do with it.
The rice jumps because something moves it.

hints: Something is moving the rice.
The rice sits on the drum skin.
What does the drum skin do when it is hit?
items.explanation: When the drum is hit, its skin vibrates. The vibrations make the rice jump, even if they are too fast to see.

items.prompt: Choose 3 things sound can travel through.

options.why: Sound needs a material to travel through. Empty space has none.

hints: Sound can travel through gases, liquids and solids.
Can you hear someone knocking on a door?
Look for the one place with nothing in it.
items.explanation: Sound travels through solids, liquids and gases, like wood, water and air. It cannot travel through empty space, where there is nothing to vibrate.

items.prompt: Astronauts on the Moon talk to each other by radio. Why do they not shout instead?

options.why: Helmets let light through. The problem is sound.

options.text: Sound travels too slowly on the Moon.
options.why: Sound cannot travel there at all, because there is no air.

options.text: There is no air on the Moon to carry sound.
Shouting is not allowed in space.
options.why: It is not a rule. Sound simply cannot travel there.

hints: Sound needs something to travel through.
What is around you when you shout at home?
Does the Moon have air?
items.explanation: Sound needs a material, like air, to travel through. The Moon has no air, so astronauts use radios.

items.prompt: Raka and Lisa make a string telephone with two cups. How does Lisa's voice reach Raka?

options.why: There is no electricity in a string telephone.

options.text: Sound only travels through the air.
options.why: Sound can travel through solids, like the string.

options.text: The cups make their own sounds.
options.why: The cups pass on Lisa's voice. They do not make it.

options.text: Her voice makes the string vibrate, and the vibrations travel to his cup.

hints: Talking makes the cup vibrate.
The string is joined to the cup.
What travels along the tight string?
items.explanation: Lisa's voice makes her cup vibrate. The vibrations travel along the tight string to Raka's cup, and he hears them.

items.prompt: The string telephone stops working when someone pinches the string. Why?

options.text: The pinch stops the string vibrating, so the vibrations cannot pass.

options.why: Pinching does not make the string longer.
The cups weigh the same as before.

options.text: Sound cannot travel through string at all.
options.why: Sound did travel through the string before the pinch.

hints: Sound travels along the string as vibrations.
What happens to vibrations when the string is held tightly?
Think about stopping a guitar string with your hand.
items.explanation: Sound travels along the string as vibrations. Pinching stops the string vibrating, so the sound cannot pass the pinch.

items.prompt: Why does music sound quieter as you walk away from the speaker?

options.text: Sound gets slower as it travels.
options.why: Sound keeps the same speed in air. It gets fainter.

options.text: Sound spreads out and gets fainter as it travels.

options.why: Your ears still work. The sound reaching them is weaker.
Sound can travel much further, but it gets fainter.

hints: The speaker is still playing just as loudly.
Think about ripples spreading in a pond.
What happens to the ripples as they spread?
items.explanation: As sound travels, it spreads out and gets fainter. Further away, less sound reaches your ears.

items.prompt: A buzzer was covered with different materials. How many decibels quieter was it with foam than with no cover?

head: Cover
Sound level (dB)
figure.alt: Table of sound levels: no cover 70 dB, paper 65 dB, wool 45 dB, foam 40 dB.

hints: Find the two numbers you need.
Quieter by how much means find the difference.
Take the foam level away from the no-cover level.
items.explanation: With no cover it was 70 dB and with foam it was 40 dB. 70 take away 40 is 30 dB, so foam muffled the sound best.

items.prompt: The loudness of a sound is measured in ___.
hints: A sound level meter shows this unit.
Its short form has two letters.
The word starts with deci.
items.explanation: Loudness is measured in decibels (dB) using a sound level meter.

items.prompt: How does a sound reach the inside of your ear?

options.text: Your ears send out sound and catch it back.
options.why: Ears do not send out sound. They receive it.

options.text: Light carries the sound into your eyes.
options.why: We hear with our ears, and light is not needed.

options.text: Vibrations travel through the air and make your eardrum vibrate.

options.why: Sound mostly reaches us through the air.

hints: Sound is a vibration.
It travels from the source through the air.
Which part inside your ear has the word drum in it?
items.explanation: The source makes the air vibrate. The vibrations travel to your ear and make your eardrum vibrate, and your brain hears a sound.

items.prompt: A music room has thick curtains, carpets and soft wall panels. Why?

options.why: Soft materials soak up sound, so they make the room quieter.
This is about sound, not electricity.
They are there to control sound.

options.text: Soft materials absorb sound and reduce echoes.

hints: Think about how sound bounces off hard walls.
Soft materials do not bounce sound back well.
What do soft materials do with sound instead?
items.explanation: Hard surfaces reflect sound and make echoes. Soft materials absorb sound, so the room sounds clearer.

items.prompt: Lightning and thunder happen at the same time. Why do you see the flash before you hear the thunder?

options.text: Light travels much faster than sound.
Thunder is made later than the lightning.
options.why: They happen together. The sound just arrives later.
Both senses are fast. The difference is in how fast light and sound travel.
It is the other way round. Light is much faster.

hints: Both start at the same place and time.
They travel to you at different speeds.
Which one wins the race to you?
items.explanation: Light travels almost a million times faster than sound. The flash reaches you almost at once, but the thunder takes longer.

items.prompt: Every sound is made when something ___.
hints: Think about a plucked guitar string.
You can feel it on your throat when you hum.
The word starts with v.
items.explanation: Sounds are made by vibrations, which are tiny movements back and forth.

items.prompt: Label the drum experiment.

figure.alt: A drum seen from the side. Small grains of rice sit on the drum skin on top. A drumstick is held above the skin on the right.

hints: Tap a label, then tap its number.
The stick hits the drum.
The grains sit on the top of the drum.
items.explanation: The stick hits the drum skin, and the skin vibrates. The rice grains jump to show the vibration.

items.prompt: Two cups are joined by a tight string. Tap the part that carries the sound between the cups.

figure.alt: A string telephone: two cups, one on each side, joined by a straight string.

hints: Sound is carried by vibrations.
Something must pass the vibrations along.
Look between the cups.
items.explanation: Voice makes the first cup vibrate. The vibrations travel along the tight string to the second cup.

items.prompt: A speaker plays music. Tap the person who hears the quietest sound.

figure.alt: A speaker on the left. Three people stand in a line to the right of it: A is closest, B is in the middle and C is the farthest away.

hints: The vibrations spread out as they travel.
Think about how far each person is from the speaker.
The farthest person gets the weakest vibrations.
items.explanation: Sound gets weaker as it travels away from its source. Person C is farthest, so C hears the quietest sound.

items.prompt: A sound meter is moved away from a speaker. Look for the pattern and complete the table.
head: Distance (m)
Loudness (dB)
hints: Compare 1 m, 2 m and 4 m.
The distance doubles each time.
The loudness drops by the same number each time the distance doubles.
items.explanation: Each time the distance doubles, the sound is 6 dB quieter. So 8 m gives 62 dB and 16 m gives 56 dB.

items.prompt: Put these in order of how fast sound travels in them, slowest first.
hints: Vibrations pass more easily when particles are close together.
Gases have the particles furthest apart.
Solids pass sound fastest.
items.explanation: Sound travels slowest in air, faster in water and fastest in a solid such as steel.

items.prompt: Can sound travel through it? Sort the cards.
hints: Sound needs something to vibrate.
Gases, liquids and solids all have particles.
Empty space has no particles.
items.explanation: Sound travels through materials that can vibrate. Empty space has nothing to vibrate, so sound cannot cross it.

items.prompt: Bayu hits a drum and then puts his hand flat on the skin. The sound stops. Why?

options.text: His hand makes the sound go away.
options.why: Hands do not remove sound, they stop what makes it.

options.text: His hand stops the skin from vibrating.

options.why: Drums do not get hot like this.
Air does not leave the drum.

hints: What makes the sound?
Think about what you feel on the skin.
Stopping the vibration stops the sound.
items.explanation: Sound needs vibrations. Resting a hand on the skin stops the vibrations, so the sound stops.

items.prompt: Tom shouts towards a cliff. Two seconds later he hears his voice again. What happened?

options.text: The cliff made a new sound.
options.why: A cliff cannot make sound by itself.

options.text: The sound was reflected by the cliff.
The sound was used up and came back.
options.why: Sound is not used up.

options.text: The sound travelled faster than light.
options.why: Sound is much slower than light.

hints: Hard surfaces can bounce sound.
A bounced sound is an echo.
The sound came back to Tom.
items.explanation: The sound hit the hard cliff and bounced back. We call this an echo.

items.prompt: Sound travels about 340 metres each second in air. How far does it travel in 3 seconds?
hints: Distance is speed times time.
Multiply 340 by 3.
340 times 3 is the same as 300 times 3 plus 40 times 3.
items.explanation: In 3 seconds the sound travels 340 × 3 = 1020 metres.

items.prompt: Choose 2 ways to make a sound quieter for a listener.

options.text: Put the buzzer in a foam-lined box

hints: Quieter means weaker vibrations reach the ear.
Distance and soft materials weaken sound.
Hitting harder and turning up do the opposite.
items.explanation: Distance and a foam box weaken the vibrations that reach the ear. Hitting harder or turning up makes it louder.

items.prompt: A sound is made by a ___. The vibrations travel through a ___ such as air, water or steel to reach our ___.
hints: Sound is a kind of movement.
It needs something to travel through.
We hear with a part of our head.
items.explanation: Vibrations make sound. They travel through a material to reach our ears.

items.prompt: Kofi covers a buzzer with four different materials. Which material is best at blocking sound?

options.why: Cardboard gave a louder reading than foam and the towel.
With no cover the sound was loudest.
The towel was good, but another material gave a lower reading.

hints: The best blocker gives the lowest reading.
Compare the four dB numbers.
Find the smallest number.
items.explanation: Foam gave the lowest reading, 52 dB. So it blocks the most sound.

head: Cover
Loudness (dB)
figure.alt: Table of loudness: no cover 80 dB, foam 52 dB, cardboard 66 dB, towel 58 dB.

items.prompt: A diver under the sea hears a boat engine. What does this show?

options.why: The diver heard the engine, so sound does travel.
Sound also travels through liquids and solids.

options.text: The diver is hearing with their eyes.
options.why: We hear with our ears.

hints: The diver is not in the air.
What is the sound travelling through?
Think about liquids.
items.explanation: Sound travels as vibrations through liquids as well as gases and solids. So the diver can hear the engine.

items.prompt: Match each instrument to the part that vibrates.
hints: Think about what you pluck, hit or blow.
Wind instruments make the air vibrate.
Drums have a stretched surface.
items.explanation: A guitar has vibrating strings and a drum has a vibrating skin. A flute makes the air vibrate and a triangle is a vibrating metal bar.

items.prompt: Sekar says a loud shout travels faster than a whisper. Is she right?

options.text: Yes, loud sounds always travel faster.
options.why: Loudness does not change the speed.

options.text: No, both travel at the same speed in the same air, but the shout is stronger and goes further.
Yes, whispers stop in the air.
options.why: Whispers travel too, only weaker.

options.text: No, loud sounds do not travel at all.
options.why: Loud sounds do travel.

hints: Compare speed and loudness separately.
The speed depends on the material it travels through.
Both are in the same air.
items.explanation: Speed depends on the material, not the loudness. A shout has bigger vibrations, so it can be heard from further away.

items.prompt: A closed wooden door still lets some sound through from the next room. How?

options.text: The sound flows through tiny holes only.
options.why: Even a solid door without holes passes some sound.

options.text: The sound goes round the planet.
options.why: It does not need to go round the planet.

options.text: The door vibrates and passes the vibrations on.
Sound goes through doors without vibrating.
options.why: All sound is made of vibrations.

hints: Sound can travel through solids.
Think about what the door does when sound hits it.
It passes the vibrations on to the air on the other side.
items.explanation: Sound makes the door vibrate a little. The door then makes the air on the other side vibrate, so you hear a quieter sound.

items.prompt: A bell rings inside a glass jar. The air is pumped out. What do you notice?

options.why: Without air, fewer vibrations reach your ear.

options.text: You see the bell move but hear almost nothing.

options.why: The bell still moves.
Sound never turns into light.

hints: Think about what sound needs to travel.
What carries the vibrations to the glass?
Remove the air and think what is left.
items.explanation: With no air there is nothing to carry the vibrations to the jar and your ear. So the sound nearly disappears.
